# EclipseGamePlatform  
A cross-platform game engine engineered for high-performance, low-latency gameplay across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Built with a focus on real-time rendering pipelines, asynchronous task scheduling, and deterministic physics simulations. This project is a personal endeavor to push the boundaries of platform-agnostic game development, leveraging modern C++ and distributed systems patterns.  

## Getting Started / Installation  
Clone the repository and initialize submodules:  
```bash  
git clone --recursive https://github.com/gabrielsouza/EclipseGamePlatform.git  
cd EclipseGamePlatform  
mkdir build && cd build  
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release  
make -j$(nproc)  
```  
Ensure your system meets the requirements: C++20 compiler, Vulkan SDK (for Windows/macOS), and X11 development headers (for Linux). The build process integrates static analysis via Clang-Tidy and unit tests via Google Test.  

## Tech Stack  
- **Rendering**: Vulkan (Windows/macOS), OpenGL 4.6 (Linux)  
- **Physics**: Bullet Physics (customized for deterministic simulation)  
- **Networking**: ENet (low-latency multiplayer core)  
- **Build**: CMake, Ninja, and CI/CD pipelines on GitLab  
- **Monitoring**: Prometheus/Grafana for real-time latency metrics  
- **Deployment**: AWS Lambda for cloud-based test environments (CI/CD)  
- **Scripting**: Python (for rapid prototyping and tooling)  
- **Infrastructure**: Terraform for reproducible dev environments  

## Usage / Examples  
Initialize the engine with a scene graph:  
```cpp  
auto engine = std::make_unique<Engine>(ECS::World::Create());  
engine->LoadScene("assets/scenes/lobby.json");  
engine->Start();  
```  
Handle input asynchronously:  
```cpp  
InputSystem::RegisterCallback([](InputEvent event) {  
    if (event.type == InputType::KeyPress && event.key == Key::Space) {  
        Player::Instance().Jump();  
    }  
});  
```  
The engine supports ECS patterns, entity-component systems, and thread-local memory pools for minimal GC overhead.

## Architecture / Design  
The architecture prioritizes modularity and deterministic behavior. A core thread pool manages physics and rendering tasks, while a dedicated IO thread handles network packets and asset loading. The rendering pipeline is decoupled into a deferred shading stage and a forward-rendering stage, with Vulkan compute shaders for post-processing.  

## Contributing  
Contributions are welcome via GitHub pull requests. Focus on performance optimizations, cross-platform compatibility, or tooling enhancements. All changes must pass CI/CD pipelines, including static analysis and unit tests.
